situation: A confirmed repair visit has passed (a second attempt after an earlier failed fix) and the system has flagged that no work results or completion update have been received from the contractor.
action: Review the case thread to see whether the contractor has sent any message that still needs a reply from the agency. If nothing is outstanding, return the request to auto mode so the standard chasers for completion or results continue, and do not escalate or re-book manually.
rationale: A missing work result often just means the contractor's update has not arrived yet, so the first step is to confirm whether the ball is in the agency's court before intervening, and otherwise let automation resume the follow-up.

situation: A landlord who is arranging communal garden works through their own contractor confirms they have received quotes and agree to proceed, but no start date has been given yet.
action: Acknowledge the landlord's approval and ask them to pass on the contractor's start date as soon as they have it. Put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Landlord' and a note that the start date is pending. Send a short update to the tenants who reported the issue, telling them a contractor has been instructed and that you will confirm the start date once you have it.
rationale: The landlord is managing the contractor, so the agency cannot schedule the works until the date comes back. Holding the job and keeping the reporting tenants informed avoids chasing too early and stops tenants wondering whether anything is happening.

situation: A contractor who completed an approved cleaning job emails to say their invoice has been sent to the agency's operator, while the request is on hold waiting for the provider and the system is prompting the operator to check whether a reply is needed or to return the request to auto mode.
action: When the contractor confirms the invoice has been sent, no reply to them is needed. Move the task to the result/completed state, mark the request as completed for final checks, and forward the invoice to the landlord with a short covering note. Record that landlord confirmation is needed, then close the request once the final checks are done.
rationale: A contractor's invoice notification is an informational closing message rather than a question, so the right response is to progress closeout and pass the invoice to the landlord instead of replying or leaving the request on hold.

situation: A contractor emails to say a job is complete and attaches a completion photo and invoice, but the attachments are unavailable or unreadable, and the system has flagged the case to check whether a reply to the provider is needed or to return it to auto mode.
action: Treat the contractor's completion email as no further reply needed to the provider. Move the task to the result stage, mark the request completed and start the final checks. If the completion photo or invoice could not be opened or isn't required, record a reason for skipping the document upload. Then flag the case for landlord confirmation before closing, and return the request to auto mode rather than chasing the contractor.
rationale: A clear completion confirmation from the contractor does not need a response, and the remaining closeout step is landlord sign-off, which automation can continue once the request is back in auto mode.

situation: A checkout-clean estimate was requested from a contractor and the job was placed on hold waiting for the provider; the contractor then replied by email with the estimate and asked to be told if the attachment had not come through.
action: When a contractor replies after a hold for provider response, open the email and confirm the estimate attachment is present and matches the requested scope (clean, removal of dumped items, carpet clean). If it is, reply to the contractor confirming receipt and telling them to proceed, record the estimate as approved, and keep the job on hold with a 'hold for works' note until the works are completed instead of returning it to auto mode.
rationale: Answering the contractor promptly with clear confirmation avoids delay, and holding the job for works stops automation from chasing or progressing it before the clean is done.

situation: A tenant reports overgrown communal garden and hedges, and the landlord replies that they have already arranged a site visit with their own contractor and are waiting on quotes for related works, so the agency does not need to source a provider.
action: Do not proceed to provider selection or dispatch. Place the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Landlord' and note the expected follow-up date. Check for any duplicate or overlapping requests for the same works. Then chase the landlord for the contractor's quote, asking them to share it once received so approval can be progressed.
rationale: When the landlord is already handling the works through their own contractor, the agency sourcing separately would duplicate effort and cut across the landlord's arrangements, so the correct step is to pause and follow up until the quote arrives.

situation: A contractor has been asked to quote for an end-of-tenancy clean after the tenant vacated, and replies asking for the check-out report to be attached to the request so they can scope the work.
action: When a contractor quoting a check-out clean asks for the check-out report, locate the report on the property record and email it to that contractor on the same job thread, referencing the job ID, without escalating or pausing for a human handoff. Keep the job on hold awaiting their estimate.
rationale: The check-out report defines the cleaning scope and condition, so supplying it promptly is a routine information request that unblocks an accurate quote.

situation: A checkout-clean request was auto-paused because the property is vacant (not tenanted), a contractor was asked to quote against the checkout report, and the contractor then replied confirming the quote has been sent.
action: When the contractor confirms their quote has been sent after a vacant-property pause, review the quote against the checkout report scope and forward it to the landlord for approval, stating that the clean is chargeable to the outgoing tenant and asking whether the contractor may proceed. Then put the job on hold as 'Waiting for Landlord' rather than returning it to auto mode, and do not send a further reply to the contractor.
rationale: A vacant-property pause needs manual handling, and the quote must have landlord sign-off before the contractor is instructed, so the job should wait on the landlord instead of resuming automatic processing.

situation: After several reminders to a contractor about booking a check-out works visit, the contractor replies with an itemised quote for the work but no appointment details, and the request had been put on hold for a quote.
action: Treat the contractor's reply as the awaited quote rather than a scheduling confirmation. Forward the itemised quote to the landlord, listing each line item and its price, and ask explicitly for approval to instruct the contractor so the property can be made ready for remarketing. Keep the request on hold until the landlord replies, and do not instruct the contractor or return the job to auto mode before approval is received.
rationale: Quote-based works need landlord sign-off before the contractor proceeds, and a contractor reply that contains a quote means the chasing for an appointment has been superseded by the approval step.

situation: A quote-required check-out works job (carpet replacement and repainting after the tenant vacated) has been assigned to a provider, who has ignored several automated reminders to book the tenant visit and has not confirmed an appointment.
action: When the system flags that several reminders have gone unanswered, check the job's communication history for any reply from the provider, such as a quote or an appointment already arranged outside the thread. If the provider is engaged and a quote is expected, put the job on hold for the quote rather than sending more automated chasers. Check whether a response to the provider is needed. If none is needed, return the job to auto mode. If the provider has still not engaged, contact them directly or reassign the job.
rationale: Repeated automated reminders add noise when the provider is already working on a quote, so a human check separates a silent provider from one who is just slow to confirm, and the job can be held or returned to automation accordingly.

situation: A contractor has replied to a quote request for check-out remedial works (replacing non-working lights and a water-damaged ceiling board), and the job is on hold awaiting the provider; the quote needs landlord sign-off before works can proceed.
action: When a contractor's quote arrives for a job on hold 'waiting for provider', treat it as the cue to act rather than just returning the job to auto: send the landlord a concise email summarising the scope as per the check-out report, the quoted price (stating whether VAT is excluded), and a clear request for permission to proceed. Then place the job on hold with the reason 'waiting for landlord'.
rationale: The quote is the blocker for the provider hold; the next dependency is the landlord's approval of the cost, so the hold reason must be updated and the landlord asked explicitly so that the job does not stall or proceed without authorisation.

situation: After a landlord received a quote for check-out works on a vacant property, they replied asking for a second subcontractor to quote for comparison, and the system had flagged the task for the agent to decide whether a response was needed or to return it to auto mode.
action: Read the landlord's reply and treat a request for a comparison quote as a prompt for manual action rather than returning the job to auto mode. Note the landlord's request, assign a new provider to obtain the second estimate, and keep the job on hold until that quote arrives. If the property shows as not tenanted and the job is auto-paused, review it manually and do not resume automation until the quote comparison is resolved.
rationale: A landlord asking for an alternative quote is a decision point that automation cannot handle, so a human must arrange the extra provider and keep control of the job until the landlord can compare quotes and approve.

situation: The agency needed a tenant's solar panel meter reading photo for a periodic landlord record, held the task until the due period, chased the tenant by email and phone, and the tenant eventually replied with the photo attached.
action: When the tenant's reply arrives with the requested meter reading photo, forward the attachment straight to the landlord, state which period the reading covers, and ask when they will next need one. Then mark the task complete without escalating or handing off to anyone else.
rationale: The task is a simple evidence-collection loop, so once the tenant supplies the photo the quickest way to close it is to pass it to the landlord with a note on the period and the next due date.

situation: A tenant promised to finish a tenant-responsible garden tidy-up and send photos the next morning, but the agency heard nothing further after several email chasers and a hold waiting on the tenant.
action: When a tenant misses a promised photo or completion deadline after written chasers, resend the request by email once more and also phone the tenant to confirm they are receiving the emails, agreeing to resend and on an alternative way to send the photos if emails still fail, then keep the job on hold awaiting the tenant's evidence.
rationale: Repeated emails with no reply may mean messages are not being delivered or seen, so a phone call quickly resolves the communication problem and gets the completion evidence needed to close the job.

situation: A routine appliance repair request is waiting on landlord approval before a contractor can be chosen, and after several days the landlord has not replied, so the system flags it for manual review.
action: When the landlord approval step has gone unanswered for the set period, do not select a provider or escalate yet. Keep the job in the landlord approval stage, extend the wait, and check for a late reply from the landlord or tenant. Once a reply arrives, review it manually before moving on to provider selection.
rationale: A routine, non-urgent repair carries little risk from a short extra wait, and the landlord's approval is required before any contractor can be instructed, so the agent should wait for the reply and read it rather than act without consent.

situation: A provider has been assigned after landlord approval and has made contact attempts with the tenant (a callback request and a failed call connection), but no booking has been confirmed and nothing in the contact requires an agency reply.
action: Review the provider's contact attempts to see whether they ask the agency for anything. If they only concern arranging access with the tenant and need no agency response, do not intervene or send new messages. Put the job on hold with the reason 'waiting for provider' and a note that the appointment is still to be booked, then let the provider and tenant sort out the visit and revisit if no booking is confirmed.
rationale: Provider-tenant call attempts are a normal part of scheduling and need no agency action, so holding with a clear note avoids duplicate chasing while keeping the job visible until the appointment is booked.

situation: A maintenance request was on hold after the tenant completed the agency's troubleshooting checks, and the landlord had already agreed in advance to an engineer attending if the fault persisted. The tenant then replied that the fault was still present.
action: When a tenant reports that troubleshooting has not fixed the fault and the landlord has already pre-approved an engineer visit, do not ask the landlord again. Confirm internally that the issue is unresolved, assign the maintenance provider, tell the tenant the provider will contact them to arrange a visit or quote, send the provider the job details with an instruction to quote and wait for approval if needed, and then return the request to auto mode.
rationale: The tenant's reply meets the condition the landlord already approved, so the job can go straight to provider assignment without delay or a duplicate approval request, and the tenant and provider both get clear next steps.

situation: A contractor attended a scheduled repair visit, but the system showed no work results afterwards and flagged the job for checking; the contractor's invoice note then described the fault found, the fix and a successful test.
action: When no work results have been logged after a completed visit, check the contractor's invoice note for the findings and outcome, and treat it as the completion record if it confirms the fault, the fix and a passing test. Move the task to Result, mark the request completed and start the final checks. Skip optional document uploads that aren't needed, recording the reason. Then request the landlord's confirmation before closing.
rationale: The invoice note can serve as proof of completion when no separate report exists, and the landlord should still confirm before the job is closed.

situation: A repair visit has been confirmed with both the tenant and the contractor, the appointment time has passed, and no completion report or work results have come back.
action: Do not close the job or assume the works were done. Place the job on hold as 'waiting on response' and chase the contractor for an outcome of the visit (attended or not, work done, follow-up needed). Check with the tenant if the contractor stays silent, and review the job again once a reply arrives.
rationale: Without a completion report from the contractor, the real status of the visit is unknown, so the job must stay open and be actively followed up rather than progressed or closed.

situation: A tenant reported a door that has become hard to shut, and the landlord replied with a known workaround from past experience and proposed deferring any contractor visit.
action: Relay the landlord's workaround to the tenant by phone and ask them to try it before any contractor is booked. If it works, tell the landlord you are closing the request unless the tenant reports the problem again, and ask the tenant to come back if it recurs. Don't send a formal response chasing approval or book a contractor, and return the request to auto mode or close it.
rationale: When the landlord supplies a workable fix for a non-urgent, recurring fault and the tenant confirms it works, a contractor visit is unnecessary. Closing with a clear route to reopen keeps costs down while protecting the tenant.

situation: A contractor assigned to a tenant-reported appliance repair has not confirmed an appointment despite several automated email and SMS reminders, then replies by email (content not captured) after the system flags that three or more reminders have gone unanswered.
action: When the contractor replies after repeated reminders, read the reply and check it gives a visit date and time slot agreed with the tenant. If it does, acknowledge it briefly, record the visit as confirmed or rescheduled with that date and slot, and send the contractor a single confirmation email with the slot, tenant contact details and a note that the tenant may request changes. Stop further chasers once the booking is confirmed. If the reply gives no date, ask the contractor for one.
rationale: Once the contractor has responded with a booking, the reminder cycle has done its job, and recording the confirmed slot and sending one clear confirmation stops redundant chasers and keeps the tenant, contractor and task status aligned.

situation: A repair request was on hold awaiting the landlord's choice of contractor, and the landlord has replied naming the contractor they want to use for the job.
action: Treat the landlord's reply as approval and as the contractor choice, so no further response to the landlord is needed. Assign the named contractor as the maintenance provider and return the request to auto mode. Then notify the tenant that the contractor will be in touch, and send the contractor the job details so they can arrange access or quote if needed.
rationale: The landlord's reply already answers the open question of who should attend, so replying again would only add noise. Assigning the provider and notifying both parties moves the job forward.

situation: A minor maintenance request (a sticking, creaking door with misaligned hinges) is awaiting landlord approval, and after several days with no response from the landlord or tenant the system flags it for manual review.
action: Chase the landlord with a fresh, tidied-up email that restates the issue concisely without the tenant's personal availability details, offers to send a contractor to fix it where possible (or quote if the work turns out to be significant) and lets the landlord say if they would rather handle it themselves. Then place the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Landlord' so it is not progressed to provider selection until they reply, and return it to auto mode once you have checked no other response is owed.
rationale: Without landlord approval the job cannot move forward, so a clear, easy-to-answer chase with explicit options prompts a decision, while the hold prevents repeated automated escalations in the meantime.

situation: A tenant reports an appliance (e.g. kitchen extractor fan) that won't turn on, and the landlord replies with a simple user-side fix, such as a separate isolator or wall switch that needs to be switched on, instead of approving a contractor visit.
action: Relay the landlord's suggested fix to the tenant in a polite email, asking them to try it and confirm whether the appliance now works. Add an internal note that the tenant check is pending, and hold off on contractor selection or scheduling until the tenant replies.
rationale: A simple tenant-side fix may resolve the issue without a contractor callout, saving cost and time, and the job should only progress to provider selection if the tenant confirms the fault persists.

situation: A contractor's email arrived after a repair visit, but the system could not extract structured data from it; on manual review it said the job was complete, the fault had resolved itself (the door had settled), and no invoice would be charged.
action: When an extraction failure flags a contractor email, read it manually and establish the outcome (completed, no fault found, no charge). Thank the contractor, tell the landlord concisely that the job is done and no invoice or payment is due, then add a closing note and close the task as completed without payment. Check the landlord message for wording errors, such as saying an invoice was needed when none was.
rationale: Manual review of unparsed provider emails prevents completion or no-charge outcomes from being missed, and a clear closeout with an accurate landlord update avoids confusion over costs and leaves no job open.

situation: A provider was assigned to a tenant's garden maintenance request after landlord approval, but repeated chaser emails asking them to confirm a tenant appointment went unanswered, and an internal flag was raised after three or more reminders.
action: When a provider has ignored three or more booking reminders and the internal flag asks you to check what is happening, stop sending identical chasers. Verify the actual status of the job (by contacting the provider or tenant through another channel, or by checking for completion evidence). Once the work is confirmed as done, send the landlord a short update saying the work is complete and will be invoiced as agreed (for example deducted from the rent). Then check whether any further reply is needed and, if not, return the request to automated handling.
rationale: Silence from a provider after repeated reminders may mean the job was already done without confirmation, so verifying the real status and closing the loop with the landlord is more useful than adding another reminder.

situation: After chasing a landlord for approval of a high-cost specialist waste removal quote, the landlord replies approving the work, and the request has been flagged by the system to check whether a response is needed or to return it to auto mode.
action: Treat the landlord's approval as the go-ahead: do not return the request to auto mode yet. Instruct the contractor to arrange the removal and keep the job on hold with a note that it is being arranged. Then contact the tenant straight away with the contractor's available dates to arrange access, asking for prompt confirmation. If phone calls go unanswered, follow up in writing, and switch the hold reason to waiting for the tenant once the access request has been sent.
rationale: Landlord approval removes the blocker, but the job still needs contractor booking and tenant access confirmed, so it needs active human-style coordination rather than being handed back to automation.

situation: A tenant asked for garden clearance, levelling and gravelling, the landlord did not respond within the chase window, and the automated process flagged the job for manual review.
action: When the landlord approval wait expires with no reply, hand the job to the responsible property manager, who should contact the landlord directly (phone or direct chase) to resolve it. Once a quote is obtained and approved, book the contractor. Before works are ordered, put the job on hold to request funds up front from the landlord to cover the invoice, and keep it on hold while waiting for the provider's start date.
rationale: Escalating a stalled approval to a named person gets a decision faster than repeated automated chasing, and securing landlord funds before works begin avoids unpaid contractor invoices.

situation: A tenant emails asking to move an already-scheduled routine property inspection to a different day because of a concern about their pet, after the visit time had already been approved and the system flagged the job for a human check on whether a response was needed.
action: Treat the tenant's rescheduling request as needing action rather than simply returning the job to auto mode: contact the tenant to agree a suitable alternative date and confirm someone will be home, then rebook the inspection into the appropriate morning or afternoon slot, cancel the original booking, and make sure the tenant receives written confirmation of the new date and time (send it manually if the system does not send one automatically).
rationale: A tenant request to change an approved appointment cannot be handled by the automation alone, and leaving the old booking in place or the tenant unconfirmed risks a failed or duplicate visit.

situation: After a routine property inspection with no issues was reported to the landlord, the landlord replied raising unrelated concerns about an unapproved tenant alteration (a pet flap fitted to a door) and asking about recovering a spare key after a lock change.
action: Read the landlord's reply to decide whether it needs a human response or can be left to automation. Because it raises a tenancy-compliance matter (an unapproved alteration) and a key-retrieval question beyond the inspection outcome, respond to the landlord directly, confirm what the inspection report did or did not cover, and arrange follow-up with the tenant on the alteration and the spare key. Only return the request to auto mode once the landlord's questions are answered or handed to the right owner.
rationale: A clean inspection result does not close the landlord's separate concerns, and returning the job to auto mode too early would leave unapproved alterations and key access unaddressed.

situation: A tenant reported a broken key with no spare held by tenant or agency, and the landlord approved the replacement and asked for extra keys for the tenant, landlord and agency.
action: Acknowledge the landlord's approval and confirm you are arranging the work. Rewrite the job description for the provider to include the landlord's specific instructions: replace the lock, supply the exact number of new keys, and state who each set is for, including that the landlord's and agency's sets must be handed to the office. Then move to provider selection, assign the provider, and tell the tenant who will attend and that the provider will contact them to arrange a visit.
rationale: Putting the landlord's exact requirements into the provider's brief at the point of approval avoids misunderstandings over key quantities and handover, and keeps all parties informed of the next steps.

situation: A confirmed repair visit has taken place, but the agency has received no work results or completion report from the contractor, so the operator has to find out what happened.
action: Phone the maintenance provider directly to ask for the job status instead of waiting for a written update. Confirm the work was completed, how any new keys will be handed over, and how the invoice will be sent, reminding them to quote the job ID in email replies. Then move the task to Result, mark the request completed, and start the final checks.
rationale: A direct call settles the missing completion information quickly and also sets out the invoicing and key-handover steps needed to close the job cleanly.

situation: A contractor reports that a minor lock/key replacement job has been completed on site, with leftover keys still to be dropped at the agency office, after earlier back-and-forth about booking the tenant appointment.
action: Reply to the contractor with a brief acknowledgement thanking them and confirming receipt, then move the task to Result, mark the request as completed and begin final checks. If no quote or other documents exist because the work was a small on-site repair, skip the document upload and record that reason, and return the request to auto mode since no further provider response is needed. Remember the contractor's promise to deliver spare keys to the office so receipt of those keys can be confirmed.
rationale: A completion message with no outstanding questions needs only an acknowledgement, and the case can be closed out and handed back to automation, with the reason for any missing quote documented for audit.

situation: A lock repair has been completed by the contractor and confirmed by phone, the request is in final checks, and the system prompts the agent to decide whether the provider needs a reply or the request can go back to auto mode, while the contractor sends a routine email with appointment/job details.
action: Review the contractor's latest email and the call notes to confirm it is only routine confirmation or job detail and the work is already confirmed complete; if no question or action is outstanding, send no reply and return the request to auto mode. Meanwhile log the key handover (new key received, added to the key records and copied) and note that any missing completion documents were skipped because the job is complete, then proceed to the remaining closeout checks such as landlord confirmation.
rationale: Replying to routine contractor emails after the work is verified adds noise, so the agent should only intervene when something is outstanding and otherwise let automation handle closeout while the physical key and record-keeping steps are finished.

situation: A contractor has been assigned to a repair and left a voicemail for the tenant to arrange access, then the system prompts the operator to decide whether a response to the provider is needed or to return the job to auto mode.
action: Don't return the job to auto mode yet. Text the tenant (twice if needed) to say the contractor has tried to reach them and give the contractor's direct number so they can call back. Put the job on hold and ask the contractor by email, with a matching SMS nudge, whether the tenant has got back to them.
rationale: A voicemail alone doesn't confirm that a booking has been made, so nudging the tenant and checking in with the contractor keeps scheduling moving and stops the job stalling unnoticed in auto mode.

situation: A tenant reports an appliance fault, the agency suggests a troubleshooting setting from the manual, and the tenant replies that the appliance has still never worked and asks for someone to inspect it.
action: When the tenant says self-help troubleshooting has failed and asks for an inspection, send a short holding reply to the tenant saying you will be back in touch. Then email the landlord asking for approval to send an appliance repair contractor to inspect, and put the job on hold awaiting the landlord's response.
rationale: Once troubleshooting is ruled out, a contractor visit needs landlord approval, and the tenant should know it is being handled without being promised a visit before that approval.

situation: A landlord was asked to approve a minor lock repair, chased by SMS, and replied with a vague go-ahead ('needs sorting fairly soon') without naming a provider, cost limit or a firm instruction.
action: Treat a clear but informal landlord go-ahead as approval to proceed, and do not send a further reply asking for confirmation. Rewrite the task description so it tells the contractor to contact the tenant, arrange a date and time to attend, and provide a quote for the fix. Assign the maintenance provider, send the tenant and contractor notification emails with the tenant's contact details and attachments, and send the contractor an SMS prompt. Then return the request to auto mode.
rationale: The landlord has already agreed to the work, so replying again only adds delay. Converting the request into a quote-and-schedule instruction lets the contractor assess the job and moves it forward without a further approval round.

situation: A landlord replies to a repair request (a recently replaced appliance that has failed) by asking that the original installing contractor be used for a free warranty service instead of a new contractor being instructed.
action: Identify the contractor who carried out the previous replacement and phone them directly to discuss the fault and warranty cover. Put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Provider' until they call back. Once the landlord approval is confirmed, send the job to that contractor as they request, and have them check the warranty status. Record each contact in a note, then assign them as the maintenance provider.
rationale: A landlord who wants warranty cover pursued should have the original installer contacted first, because it may avoid a charge, and the installer must be given the job formally before they can verify the warranty.

situation: A maintenance request has been completed and closed out administratively (keys returned, task marked complete without payment, invoices held in the contractor's own system), but a tenant then emails asking for an update on a different, previously reported issue, while a system prompt asks the operator to check whether a response is needed before returning the request to auto mode.
action: Read the tenant's latest message and compare it with the job on this request. If it concerns a different issue from the completed work, do not reopen or act on it here; make sure it is tracked under its own request or the existing one for that issue, and send the tenant a brief acknowledgement only if none has been given. Once you have confirmed that no reply is outstanding on this request, return it to auto mode.
rationale: Closing out a finished job should not swallow an unrelated tenant query, and checking for an outstanding response before handing back to automation ensures the tenant is not left unanswered while the completed request stays cleanly closed.

situation: A repair was carried out by a provider under warranty, the tenant confirmed the fix appeared to work, and the provider emailed confirming completion at no charge, after the job had been held awaiting the provider and the system prompted a check on whether any response was needed.
action: Treat the provider's completion email as final confirmation, record a brief note that the repair was done under warranty with no charge, mark the task completed without payment, and return the request to auto mode. Do not send a reply to the provider or contact the landlord, as no response or approval is needed.
rationale: A warranty repair with tenant confirmation and no cost leaves nothing to approve, pay or chase, so the correct step is to document it and close the job cleanly instead of generating unnecessary communication.

situation: A maintenance request was paused while awaiting landlord approval to send the agency's usual appliance contractor, and the landlord has since replied with a clear, unconditional approval.
action: Read the landlord's reply and, if it is an unambiguous approval, record it as approved and return the request to auto mode with no further reply to the landlord. Then move to provider selection, assign the proposed contractor, email the tenant to say the contractor will contact them to arrange a visit, and send the contractor the job details and tenant contact information.
rationale: A clear approval needs no further response to the landlord, so the job should resume automatically and go straight to contractor assignment and notifications to avoid delays.

situation: After the system auto-sent appointment confirmations for a repair, the tenant phoned to say the date in the notifications conflicted with the date they had already agreed directly with the contractor, and asked which was correct.
action: Reply to the tenant to apologise for the confusion and tell them the date they agreed directly with the contractor is the one to follow, rather than the date in the automated notification. Then put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Provider' so the contractor can confirm the date, instead of returning it to auto mode.
rationale: Automated confirmations can be sent with a date that does not match what the contractor and tenant arranged directly, so the contractor's agreed date should take priority and the job should wait for the provider's confirmation before automation resumes.

situation: A maintenance job was resolved by the tenant's own DIY fix and closed, but the tenant then emailed again with an unrelated non-maintenance query (about parking space availability) that landlords/contractors can't answer.
action: When a tenant sends a new non-repair enquiry after a job has closed, do not ignore it or treat it as part of the closed repair. Take the first step yourself: contact the relevant third party (e.g. block management) on the tenant's behalf to gather the information, email the tenant to confirm you have done so and will update them, and only then leave the original job closed.
rationale: Acting on the enquiry immediately and keeping the tenant informed gives a good service experience and avoids handing off or reopening the repair job before the agency has done its own first action.

situation: After landlord approval and provider assignment on a plumbing request, the landlord sent only a brief acknowledgement that needed no reply, and the system prompted the operator to decide whether a response was needed or to return the job to auto mode.
action: Read the landlord's message to confirm it is only an acknowledgement with no question or instruction, so no reply is needed. Then switch the job back to auto mode so the automated provider chasing continues, and watch for the provider confirming a tenant appointment.
rationale: Replying to a simple thanks adds noise, while returning the job to auto mode lets reminders and follow-ups resume, which keeps the request moving toward booking.

situation: A landlord replied to a repair request saying they will sort the issue themselves with their own contractor, so the agency no longer needs to arrange works but still needs to know when the job is done.
action: Read the landlord's reply to check whether it needs a response; if it only confirms they will handle the repair, send no further reply. Put the request on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Landlord' and a comment saying it is held awaiting the landlord's contractor to complete. If the tenant or landlord later gives no update, chase the landlord politely for progress and keep the hold in place until the contractor reports completion.
rationale: When the landlord takes ownership of the repair, the agency's role changes from instructing works to monitoring them, so the request must stay paused rather than return to auto mode, and the landlord must be chased so the job does not stall unnoticed.

situation: A tenant reported damage to a bathroom fixture and the agency asked how it happened; the tenant said it was pre-existing at move-in. The case was then held awaiting the contractor to arrange an appointment, with no contractor contact for some time.
action: When a held job is waiting on the contractor to book an appointment and there has been no contact, check whether the contractor is unavailable (for example on annual leave) and has returned. If so, chase them for an update through the shared contractor communication channel. Keep the job on hold until they reply, then record the outcome, such as the job being done and no quote needed, and move the task to its result stage.
rationale: Proactively chasing a silent contractor once they are available keeps the job moving, and recording the outcome closes the loop without needless escalation.

situation: A contractor who missed a confirmed appointment and was rebooked has emailed to report the plumbing job completed (part replaced, tenants confirming the other fault is fine), while the request was on hold awaiting the provider and flagged to check whether a response is needed before returning to auto mode.
action: When a contractor reports completion after a rescheduled or missed visit, confirm the report covers all reported faults and that the tenant has not raised any outstanding issue. If no reply to the contractor is needed, record that the landlord pays the contractor directly, close the task as completed without agency payment, and return the request to auto mode.
rationale: A completion report that addresses every fault needs no further chasing, and noting the landlord's direct payment arrangement keeps the agency from processing an invoice it will not pay.

situation: After a plumbing visit was booked and confirmed with the tenant and contractor, the contractor's email reply could not be parsed by the system and was flagged for manual review, with no usable content available.
action: When a provider's email cannot be extracted, manually review the original message or check with the contractor directly to establish what it said. If it indicates the job is complete, move the task to the results/closeout stage. Put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Provider' and note that the contractor reports completion and the invoice is awaited. Do not treat the unreadable email as a no-op or re-send appointment messages.
rationale: An unparseable contractor email may contain a completion notice or other status change, so a human check keeps the task in the right stage and ensures the invoice is chased rather than lost.

situation: A minor repair request was on hold awaiting landlord approval, the system prompted the operator to check whether a response to the landlord was needed, and the landlord replied with a brief, clear approval to go ahead.
action: Read the landlord's reply and, if it is a clear approval, do not send any further response to the landlord. Record the approval, return the request to auto mode, and move on to provider selection. Add the landlord's cost guidance to the job description, such as assuming the job is simple and cheap but quoting if it is large, so the assigned contractor and tenant see it. Then assign a provider and send the tenant and contractor notifications.
rationale: A short unambiguous approval needs no reply, and passing the landlord's scope and cost expectations to the contractor keeps the job moving without extra back-and-forth.

situation: After a quote was sent to the landlord for approval and chased once, the landlord replied with only a thumbs-up emoji and the request was flagged to check whether a response was needed or to return it to auto mode.
action: Treat a brief affirmative reply such as a thumbs-up emoji as landlord approval of the quote already put to them. Do not send the landlord a further response. Instead, instruct the contractor straight away to proceed at the quoted price, restating the work and the quoted cost, then put the job on hold with the reason 'Waiting for Provider' until the contractor confirms scheduling or completion.
rationale: The landlord's approval was clear and nothing further was needed from them, so the next step is to move the job forward with the contractor rather than ask for clarification or return the job to auto mode.

situation: A contractor's quote for follow-on plumbing works was sent to the landlord, the request was held awaiting their reply, and the landlord has now replied approving the quote.
action: Read the landlord's reply to confirm it is a clear approval. Attach the approved quote to the job record, log that the landlord approved it, and move the task on to the next stage. No further reply to the landlord is needed, so release the hold and return the request to auto mode. Send the tenant a short email saying the maintenance provider will contact them to schedule the approved work, and remind them to tell the provider about any pets.
rationale: A clear landlord approval needs no further response, so recording it, keeping the tenant informed and handing the job back to automation lets the contractor be booked without delay.

situation: The landlord has approved the agency instructing a contractor for a minor plumbing repair, and the agency has assigned a provider and sent notifications to the tenant and the contractor, after which the system prompts a check on whether any response to the provider is needed.
action: After the landlord approves instructing a contractor, assign the maintenance provider, email the tenant with the provider name and what to expect, and send the contractor the job details, tenant contact and quote-approval conditions. Then check whether the provider needs any further reply; if the instruction already covers everything, return the request to auto mode rather than sending more messages.
rationale: The instruction email to the contractor already contains the contact details, scope and approval conditions, so no extra response is needed and the case can safely resume automated handling until the provider replies.

situation: A contractor's completion email with an attached invoice could not be machine-extracted, so the agent flagged it for manual review; the repair had been completed on site with a call-out charge only.
action: When a contractor's completion email cannot be parsed, read it manually to confirm the outcome and charges, then forward the invoice to the landlord with a brief summary stating that the job was fixed on site and what was charged. Check that the property address in the message matches the job, mark the request completed, and record that the invoice was sent to the landlord if it is not uploaded to the system. Keep the task open for final checks until the landlord confirms.
rationale: Extraction failures should not stall closeout, and manual handling still needs accurate details and landlord sign-off on the cost before the job is closed.

situation: A minor plumbing repair (low shower pressure and loose hose) was being handled by the landlord supplying parts and fitting them himself, the tenant acknowledged the update with a simple thank-you, and the agency was left waiting for the landlord to confirm the work was done.
action: When the tenant's reply is only an acknowledgement (e.g. thanks) and needs no response, do not reply further; keep the job on hold awaiting the landlord, chase the landlord by phone to confirm they received the photo and have completed the repair, record their confirmation in a note, and then close the job as completed without payment.
rationale: A courtesy reply from the tenant requires no action, while the real outstanding item is the landlord's confirmation that the self-managed repair is finished, and with no contractor involved there is no invoice to process.
